details:
**Highest peak in North America**
Denali, in Alaska's Alaska Range, is the tallest mountain in North America. A 2015 survey measured it at 20,310 feet, about 10 feet shorter than the earlier figure. It is the northernmost of the "Seven Summits" (the highest peaks on each continent) and the third most topographically prominent peak on Earth, after Everest and Aconcagua.

**"The High One" (Koyukon Athabaskan name)**
The name Denali comes from the Koyukon Athabaskan language and means "the high one" or "the tall one." The mountain lies in the ancestral homeland of the Koyukon people.

**Mount McKinley and the renamings**
In 1896, gold prospector William Dickey, who was exploring near the Susitna River, named the peak for William McKinley, who went on to win that year's presidential election and became the 25th U.S. president. In August 2015, the Obama administration, through Interior Secretary Sally Jewell, officially restored the name Denali. In 2025, the federal government changed the name back to Mount McKinley, although the national park keeps the name Denali.

**Kahiltna Glacier**
The longest glacier in the Alaska Range. It flows down Denali's southwest side between Mount Foraker and Mount Hunter, and its upper reaches serve as the base camp and starting point for most climbing expeditions.

**West Buttress Route**
The most popular and least technical route to the summit, beginning on the Kahiltna Glacier. Bradford Washburn pioneered it in 1951; he was not the first to climb the mountain.

**Frederick Cook and "Fake Peak"**
Explorer Frederick Cook falsely claimed to have made the first ascent of the mountain in 1906. His summit photo was actually taken on a much smaller outcrop near Ruth Glacier, which is now called "Fake Peak."

**Chris McCandless and Into the Wild**
Christopher McCandless, the subject of Jon Krakauer's book Into the Wild, starved to death in 1992 in an abandoned bus along the Stampede Trail near Denali National Park. The bus drew so many hikers, some of whom had to be rescued, that it was airlifted away in 2020.

**Churchill Peaks (North and South summits)**
Denali has two summits, together named the Churchill Peaks after Winston Churchill. The South Peak is the true summit and is roughly 850 feet higher than the North Peak.

**Denali National Park and Preserve**
The national park around the mountain, formerly called Mount McKinley National Park. Its single road, about 92 miles long and closed to most private vehicles, leads past the Eielson Visitor Center to Wonder Lake, a classic viewpoint for the mountain. A 2021 landslide at Pretty Rocks closed part of the road.

**1913 first ascent (Hudson Stuck, Harry Karstens, Walter Harper)**
The first confirmed ascent of the South (true) summit was made in 1913 by an expedition led by Archdeacon Hudson Stuck and Harry Karstens. Walter Harper, an Alaska Native member of the party, was the first person to stand on the summit.

**Mount Foraker and Mount Hunter**
Two nearby major peaks of the Alaska Range. The Kahiltna Glacier flows between them, and Foraker is the second-highest peak in the range.

**Ruth Glacier and the Moose's Tooth**
Ruth Glacier flows southeast from Denali through the dramatic Great Gorge. The Moose's Tooth is a striking granite peak beside the glacier, and Fake Peak is also nearby.

**Talkeetna**
A small town south of the mountain that serves as the main staging point for climbing expeditions. Bush pilots fly climbers from there to the Kahiltna Glacier base camp.

**Muldrow Glacier**
A large glacier on Denali's northeast side, named for topographer Robert Muldrow, who measured the mountain's height in 1898. It began a rare "surge" in 2021, moving dozens of times faster than normal.

**Mount Logan**
The highest peak in Canada, in Yukon. Before Denali was measured at over 20,000 feet, Logan had been thought to be the tallest mountain in the region.
